The Federal Aviation Administration issued the certification for the Boeing 737 MAX-10, a decisive step that clears the path for the aircraft’s entry into commercial service and expands the fleet capacity available to U.S. airlines. This regulatory approval stands alongside the agency’s adoption of a new airworthiness directive for certain Boeing 737 series airplanes, signaling a continued focus on fleet safety and compliance [FAA issued the certification](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/federal-aviation-administration-issues-certification-boeing-737-max-10) [FAA adopted the directive](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/19/2026-21332/airworthiness-directives-the-boeing-company-airplanes).

In the advanced air mobility sector, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy announced the first-ever Special Airworthiness Market Survey Certificate for eVTOL aircraft, establishing a new regulatory framework for this emerging technology. Concurrently, Duffy announced New Mexico’s first demonstration flight under the USDOT’s Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing Integration Pilot Program, marking a tangible milestone in the integration of these aircraft into the national airspace system [Duffy announced the certificate](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/trumps-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-announces-first-ever-special-airworthiness) [Duffy announced the flight](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/trumps-transportation-secretary-sean-p-duffy-announces-new-mexicos-first-advanced-air).

Security concerns along the U.S.-Mexico border have prompted the FAA to impose a ban on unauthorized drones in the region, a measure cited as a response to cartel threats. This restriction, reported to remain in effect through 2027, represents a significant shift in airspace management and counter-UAS policy, prioritizing national security over open access in border zones [FAA imposed the ban](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqwFBVV95cUxOYUk3MFJkMVBOQWlWUUZCa3I5STJaWV81bVJFNUc1WkpYODBYX0RUR2l3SzhjZVo2Q0pkbWhjWmxmS3NsdXhpVUVMU2xJS0hCYm9EbWlhZmJONE83aTZQalppTGJNTEROcmtmN2gyZmlUUnB6SDJjOF9Wc0xPSWxUam5UM0hjUWNRRkpCUy1FLTBUbVdxdmE0Q2VBNTF3NnFlVVBLeFJKNnNtcVk?oc=5) [FAA restricted drones](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuAFBVV95cUxPc1pjSzN4X2UteGJjMkRFdFFrYk13MHl5c1BGVmRma0NkZjJZc0tUZTVNaFdpMDg5TEx5QjdFTW03LUJnZHNmdFctX3BvNTJNcXZFYVgtZzdtcHdmOGFhWjc2X2NPbjI4c0dGMVNfNG5jQjNwMDdCRGpzbWVha05DQkJGSF92ZlJXNUV4c1o2SldrWlpHNUFpSmEwRks4MjNvUm5PVnpGS1JIeFlxM2g0MzJMU1RWTHpv?oc=5).

Regulatory scrutiny of autonomous vehicles remains intense, with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opening a probe into Tesla robotaxis for speeding and ignoring school zones. This investigation adds to ongoing questions regarding Cybercab scaling and safety, while the FAA also proposed a $351,000 civil penalty against Creamer Pilot Services for alleged unauthorized passenger-carrying operations [NHTSA opened the probe](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMic0FVX3lxTE8zQThsSmRPZXVoOHRjRmt6QllXU1lQYkJuQ0o1ckdVX2lDbmg0Nk4yTnlyamxqU0lnanc2Qk1sdVJZMlFRUE1BN1lwSFZiVzl3U2NBWFBWN1I5VDA4cEZFUHBEdkNYb1JhLS0xbmtCNlduQ1E?oc=5) [FAA proposed the penalty](https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-proposes-351000-fine-against-creamer-pilot-services-alleged-unauthorized-passenger).
